source: Chi, Feltovich, Glaser (1981) Categorization and representation of physics problems by experts and novices (as described in Mason & Singh 2016 and Wolf et al 2012)
finding: Founding study. Novices sorted mechanics problems by surface features (ramp, spring, pulley). Experts sorted by principle. Only secondary accounts were read.
numbers: 8 novices (just finished 1 semester of calculus physics) and 8 physics PhD students. Novices used springs 75%, inclined plane 50%, kinetic energy 50%, pulleys 38%. Experts used springs 25%, none of the others.
limits: Tiny N. Problem set is lost; only 7 problems are known. Instruction was sort by similarity of solution, multiple categories allowed, no pencil.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim for S2: good representation names the governing principle, not the story.

source: Mason & Singh (2016) Categorization of Mechanics Problems by Students in Large Introductory Physics Courses: A Comparison with the Chi, Feltovich, and Glaser Study
finding: Large in-class re-run with 25 problems (7 from Chi). Contrary to Chi, many intro students chose expert categories and few chose surface ones.
numbers: Classes of 109, 114 (algebra) and 180 (calculus). Chi novices: 0% chose Newton 2, energy, linear kinematics. Here, 18% Newton 2, 31% energy, 28% circular motion, 44% linear kinematics (7 Chi problems, algebra class). Ramp chosen by 19% (Chi problems), 24% (others) vs 50% in Chi. Kinetic energy at most 16% vs 50%.
limits: Chi problems were harder for students than non-Chi ones. Students were concurrently enrolled; Chi volunteers maybe not. Algebra class likely worse than calculus class.
agent_relevance: The novice=surface picture is partly an artefact of sample and problem set. Do not assume a weak solver always sorts by surface.

source: Mason & Singh (2016) Assessing Expertise in Introductory Physics Using Categorization Task
finding: Calculus-based intro students overlap strongly with physics grad students on good categorisation. Expertise is a wide distribution, not two groups.
numbers: Version I mean share of 25 problems in good categories: calculus group 34.4%, algebra group 18.7%. 21 grad students and 7 faculty compared. Two algebra classes did not differ (ANOVA p=0.90 over 15 shared problems; t-tests p 0.42-0.96).
limits: Hand rating of categories good/moderate/poor by 3 faculty, agreement above 95%. Single university.
agent_relevance: Measure representation quality on a graded scale, not as expert/novice binary.

source: Mason & Singh (2016) Assessing Expertise (faculty vs graduate students)
finding: Grad students are not true experts here. Faculty categorised much better than grad students. Chi et al used grad students as experts.
numbers: 21 grad students and 7 faculty. Large difference grad vs faculty; large overlap calc students vs grad students.
limits: Faculty N=7.
agent_relevance: The expert reference class matters. A model compared with a mid-level expert can look expert-like by accident.

source: Mason & Singh (2016) Assessing Expertise: think-aloud interviews
finding: Students sometimes know the principle but pick a surface-flavoured label (friction) on purpose. They find 'force' too vague and want to address details.
numbers: 4 intro students interviewed, plus a few grad students and professors.
limits: Interviews not fully analysed in this paper.
agent_relevance: A surface label may be a choice of grain size, not a failure to see structure. Ask for the principle, not only the label.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) Empirical approach to interpreting card-sorting data
finding: Standard descriptive statistics (number of categories, graph measures) failed to separate experts and novices. Most variance was sorting style, not expertise.
numbers: 18 physics professors and 23 novices, 50 problems. Number of categories: experts 10.8 +/- 4.5, novices 11.4 +/- 4.4. KS tests on 3-cycles, clique size, diameter, path length: no difference. PCA of 41 sorters: first two components about 87% of variance; PC1 = stacker vs spreader (not expertise); expertise only on PC2.
quote: most variance in the data is not related to the expert or novice identity of the sorters
limits: One university, one problem set. Authors say sorting may reflect personal filing habits.
agent_relevance: Card sorting is a noisy measure of representation. Use problem-specific checks, not summary counts.

source: Wolf, Dougherty, Kortemeyer (2012) Rigging the deck: Selecting good problems for expert-novice card-sorting experiments
finding: Whether experts and novices differ depends strongly on which problems are in the set. Replications often fail for this reason.
numbers: Same 18 professors and 23 novices, 50 problems. Problem features explained 35.9% (5-problem subsets) and 42.7% (10-problem subsets) of discrimination. Share explained by feature group (10-problem): chapter 41.4%, procedural task type 30.4%, difficulty 22.8%, other 5.4%. Easy problems discriminated better than hard ones.
quote: efforts to replicate the study frequently fail, since the ability to distinguish experts from novices turns out to be highly sensitive to the problem set
limits: Subset analysis is not the same as running the experiment with fewer cards. More than half of variance unexplained.
agent_relevance: Test sets for representation must be built with known principle-by-surface crossings, or the test measures nothing.

source: Veldhuis (1986, 1990) as summarised in Wolf et al 2012
finding: First replication attempt. Sets that mimicked Chi gave no clear result. Only sets built with an explicit principle-by-surface matrix showed experts sorting by principle and novices showing mixed behaviour.
numbers: 94 intro novices, 5 intermediates, 20 professors; 4 problem sets. Sets 3 and 4 were rigged (4x4 and 2x2 grid of principle by surface feature).
limits: Secondary account only; original not opened.
agent_relevance: A crossed design (same surface, different principle, and the reverse) is the way to test a representation step.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1989) The relation between problem categorization and problem solving among experts and novices
finding: Experiment 1: experts chose the same-principle problem more often than novices, but surface similarity hurt both. Novices were not purely surface-driven.
numbers: 45 novices, 8 PhD physicists plus 2 advanced students. Deep-structure choice: experts 78%, novices 59% (F(1,53)=28.78, p<.0001). Surface-trap items (S-D): experts 66%, novices 26%. Neutral items (N-SD): experts 91%, novices 87%. Novice S-D 95% CI 20-32%, well above the 0% a pure surface rule predicts.
limits: Similarity-judgment task, mechanics only.
agent_relevance: Even experts are pulled by surface cues. A surface-trap check is a useful test of any representation step.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1989) Experiment 2
finding: Among novices of equal experience, those who reasoned by principle categorised more like experts and solved more problems. Link between representation and score.
numbers: 44 novices split by reasoning: surface 17, mixed 16, principle 11. Categorisation correct: 56%, 63%, 69%; experts 95%. Problem-solving score: 14%, 32%, 57%, F(2,41)=16.19, p<.0001. Principle-use frequency vs score r=.63; partial r=.505 with maths ability removed; r=.613 with SAT-M as the control.
quote: principles play a fundamental role in the organization of conceptual and procedural knowledge for good problem solvers at all levels
limits: Correlational. Principle users still named wrong principles: 38% of the time they identified an inappropriate one. Novices who cited a principle used it correctly only about 60% of the time.
agent_relevance: Attempting a principle step helps, but only if the principle is right. Check the named principle, do not trust it.

source: Hardiman, Dufresne, Mestre (1989) Experiment 2 reasons given
finding: Experts nearly always gave principle reasons. Novices in the mixed and surface groups seldom did.
numbers: Experts cited principles 93-98% of the time. Novices: principle group 70%, mixed 23%, surface group 6%.
limits: Reasons coded blind by first author only.
agent_relevance: Ask for the written reason alongside the label; reasons are the audit trail.

source: Engle & Chi (2002) Categorization of Emergent Processes by Students at Different Levels of Expertise
finding: Card-sort extension to cross-domain science problems. Expertise gave no reliable separation of emergent from non-emergent processes.
numbers: Separation score doctoral .58, single majors .53, double majors .73; no differences reliable.
limits: Short proceedings paper, small groups, preliminary.
agent_relevance: Deep-structure sorting is domain bound. It does not generalise to all knowledge types.

source: Singh (2009) TA categorisation study, as summarised in Wolf et al 2012
finding: Grad TAs asked to categorise as themselves and as their students overestimated how well intro students would do. Faculty did best.
numbers: Described as: TAs-as-students did better than real students; faculty best. No exact numbers read.
limits: Second-hand account only.
agent_relevance: An expert simulating a novice leaks expertise. Same likely for a strong model told to play a weak solver.

source: Lin & Singh (2010) quantum mechanics categorisation, as summarised in Wolf et al 2012
finding: In quantum mechanics, experts varied more and even the faculty rating panel disagreed on what is a good category.
numbers: 22 junior/senior majors vs 6 faculty; 3-member faculty panel.
limits: Second-hand account.
agent_relevance: In less settled domains, no single correct representation exists. Allow more than one.

source: Schoenfeld & Herrmann (1982) Problem perception and knowledge structure in expert and novice mathematical problem solvers
finding: Math experts sort by structure; novices by surface. Cited in Hardiman et al as agreeing with Chi. Original not opened.
numbers: None read; only citation context seen.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Shows the effect outside physics.

source: Zheng et al (2023) Take a Step Back: Evoking Reasoning via Abstraction in Large Language Models
finding: Ask the model first for the governing principle, then solve. This is an LLM version of principle-first representation. Large gains on physics and chemistry.
numbers: MMLU high-school physics: PaLM-2L 66.4% to 73.2%; GPT-4 69.4% to 84.5% (GPT-4 + CoT 82.9%). Chemistry: PaLM-2L 70.9% to 81.8%; GPT-4 80.9% to 85.6% (CoT 85.3%). TimeQA +27, MuSiQue +7 (PaLM-2L).
limits: Few-shot demos for abstraction. Gain over strong CoT with GPT-4 is small on chemistry (85.3 vs 85.6) and 1.6 points on physics.
agent_relevance: Direct support for an S2 step that names the principle before any attempt.

source: Zheng et al (2023) Step-Back error analysis
finding: After the principle is stated, nearly all remaining errors are in the reasoning, not the principle. Step-back also breaks some correct answers.
numbers: Physics: fixes 20.5% of baseline errors, introduces 11.9% new ones. More than 90% of the remaining errors occur in the Reasoning step.
limits: PaLM-2L only for error analysis.
agent_relevance: Principle step is cheap and rarely the bottleneck, but 11.9% harm means it needs a check, not blind trust.

source: Zheng et al (2023) Step-Back ablation on number of exemplars
finding: Abstraction skill is easy to teach a model: very few demonstrations are enough.
numbers: Paper states very few exemplars are needed (ablation, TimeQA). Exact counts not recorded.
limits: Exact exemplar counts not recorded here.
agent_relevance: No heavy training needed; a short instruction and one example may do.

source: Shi et al (2023) Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context
finding: Adding one irrelevant sentence to grade-school maths problems sharply cuts robustness. LLM analogue of surface capture.
numbers: GSM-IC-4K, code-davinci-002, exemplars without distractors. CoT micro accuracy 72.4%, but macro accuracy (a base problem solved under all distractors) only 6.0%. Least-to-most: micro 77.5%, macro 18.0%. Self-consistency raises CoT micro to 88.1% and macro to 30.0%. Ignore-irrelevant instruction: CoT micro 77.8%, macro 15.0%.
limits: Old models (code-davinci-002, text-davinci-003). Single distractor sentence.
agent_relevance: Representation should list what is relevant and drop the rest; test with distractor insertion.

source: Shi et al (2023) GSM-IC mitigations
finding: Fixes help but do not remove the problem: self-consistency, an ignore-irrelevant instruction, and exemplars that contain irrelevant context.
numbers: Exemplars with irrelevant context: CoT micro 76.8% (macro 14.0%) vs 72.4% (6.0%) without. LTM+SC reached micro 93.4%, macro 45.0%.
limits: Same caveats as above.
agent_relevance: Include a distractor-aware example in any representation prompt.

source: Mirzadeh et al (2025) GSM-Symbolic: Understanding the Limitations of Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Changing only numbers or names changes accuracy. Adding a clause that looks relevant but is not (GSM-NoOp) causes large drops even for strong models.
numbers: Drop up to 65% (Phi-3-mini) on GSM-NoOp; o1-preview about -17.5 points. Gemma2-9B best-to-worst gap across sets above 12%. Eight shots of the same question did not repair NoOp performance.
limits: Authors interpretation (pattern matching, not reasoning) is a hypothesis. Results are for 2024 models.
agent_relevance: Evidence that models map text cues to operations; the representation step must test relevance by meaning.

source: Mirzadeh et al (2025) GSM-Symbolic: clause count
finding: Accuracy falls and variance rises as clauses are added, with the drop rate accelerating.
numbers: Reported across all models; exact per-model numbers in figures not recorded.
limits: Figures not read numerically.
agent_relevance: Long problems need decomposition before representation.

source: Lampinen et al (2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: LLMs and humans both reason better when the content supports the logical answer; content leaks into logical judgment, as surface cues do for novices.
numbers: Tasks: NLI, syllogisms, Wason. Humans called invalid syllogisms valid 90% of the time when the conclusion was believable (Evans et al, as cited). Content effects small in NLI, moderate in syllogisms, large in Wason.
limits: Model-by-model numbers in figures not recorded.
agent_relevance: Swapping content for abstract symbols is a cheap way to expose cue-driven answers.

source: Webb, Holyoak, Lu (2023) Emergent Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: GPT-3 matched or beat students on abstract matrix and string analogy but did worse on story analogies where relations must win over shared entities.
numbers: Digit matrices: GPT-3 beat humans (N=40), OR=1.88, p=0.005. Story analogies (N=54 humans): humans better, OR=0.37, p=0.0003. GPT-3 far-analogy choice not significant (p=0.065); near p=0.0039. GPT-4 preliminary: better.
limits: GPT-3 era; GPT-4 results preliminary.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain structure matching is where models used to fail. Re-test on current models.

source: Yasunaga et al (2024) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Prompting the model to recall related problems before solving helps, about +4% on average, and beats fixed exemplars on mixed-topic maths and code.
numbers: Abstract: average +4% accuracy. GSM8K GPT-3.5 in the 75-78% range across arms; MATH GPT-3.5 33.0% (5-shot) vs 33.9-37.3% self-generated. Table cell alignment was garbled in text extraction, so individual cells are approximate.
limits: Self-generated exemplars are only as good as the model's recall. Gain is small for GPT-3.5 on GSM8K.
agent_relevance: Recalling a same-principle problem is a retrieval-by-structure move; tie it to the principle name, not topic words.

source: Cross-study synthesis: Shi 2023, Mirzadeh 2025, Zheng 2023 (this agent)
finding: Models resemble Chi novices in being captured by cues in the text. Explicit prompting to name the principle or list relevant facts partly fixes it, but not fully.
numbers: Step-Back +7 to +15 points on physics; GSM-IC macro 6% to 45% depending on method; NoOp drops up to 65%.
limits: Synthesis across different models and tasks; not a controlled comparison.
agent_relevance: Design S2 as: name principle, list givens, mark distractors, then check by a counter-framing.
